title: Sanity-Checking Fragile IT Decisions
author: Henriques, Artur
summary: Artur Henriques offers a practical diagnostic method for IT and engineering leaders to spot decisions built on unexamined data before those decisions get locked in. His first warning sign is estimate variance: an estimate range wider than roughly 10-20% (his example is a feature quoted as 'around 20 to 40 days,' a 100% variance) signals that no engineering lead or manager actually pressure-tested the number, and he explicitly connects this pattern to the growing habit of copy-pasting an LLM's estimate without scrutiny. His second method is a standing checklist of basic questions to run against any cost or service assessment — SLAs, support response times, backup and recovery timelines, and whether costs are CAPEX or OPEX — designed to catch the assumptions salespeople benefit from leaving unstated. His third focus is the specific risk of short-duration contracts, arguing that a one-year term gives a vendor an easy opening to raise prices at renewal, and that leaders should negotiate cost-increase caps and reversibility clauses into contracts rather than discovering the exposure later. The piece is aimed squarely at building a habit of sanity-checking numbers and assumptions before they are used to justify a decision, particularly as AI-generated estimates enter the pipeline unchecked.
points: An estimate range wider than roughly 10% (his illustrative example: a feature quoted as 'around 20 to 40 days,' a 100% variance) is treated as a reliable signal that no engineering lead or manager actually pressure-tested the number.
Henriques explicitly names a new failure pattern: someone asks an LLM for a cost or time estimate and copy-pastes the output into a plan without any sanity check.
He recommends a reusable checklist for any IT service or cost assessment covering SLAs, support response times, whether installation and backup costs are included, and whether spend is CAPEX or OPEX.
On multi-year commitments, he warns that one-year contracts are especially exposed to price increases at renewal because the short term gives a vendor an easy negotiating opening.

His recommended mitigation is negotiating explicit caps on cost increases and reversibility clauses into contracts up front, rather than discovering the exposure only when a vendor proposes a renewal increase.
quotes: The real problem arises later in the decision-making process: information is presented to justify a choice, but it never underwent rigorous analysis or critique.
However, when an estimate carries a variance greater than 10%, it shows something was missed. For example, estimating that a feature will take "around 20 to 40 days" represents a 100% variance.

High cost variance is almost always a symptom of poor planning and shallow analysis. Now, we are seeing this exact issue spill straight out of raw AI prompts. Someone asks an LLM for an estimate and copy-pastes the output without a second thought.

Assumptions are always the mother of all f%ck-ups. A good way to clear those assumptions is to prepare a checklist of items that you want to make sure are included in a given cost or service assessment.
This can be potentially problematic for 1-year contracts. Since the duration is very short, the vendor can easily propose increasing the price in the next negotiation.
If the vendor cannot be easily changed, you are much better off negotiating a longer contract term with proper renewal and reversibility clauses.
